opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think this is a really useful lens, because it exposes an assumption hiding inside a lot of the headline numbers. When people say "AI makes this task ten times faster," they're usually measuring the bit of the work that happens at the keyboard: drafting the code, writing the summary, searching the literature. But a lot of what makes human intellectual work actually work happens off the clock.

Take sleep. There's decent evidence that sleep plays a role in consolidating what we've learned, and many people have had the experience of going to bed stuck on a problem and waking up with the answer. Or the shower thought, or the walk where something finally clicks. Those processes run at biological speed. You can't hand them to a model and get them back in a tenth of the time. So if a meaningful share of the real progress on a hard problem happens in that incubation period, then speeding up the conscious, active part gives you much less than the headline multiplier suggests.

It's essentially Amdahl's law applied to cognition. If 50% of what produces a breakthrough is the slow, unconscious, overnight part, then even an infinite speedup on the other 50% only gets you a factor of two overall. And the bottleneck becomes the thing you couldn't accelerate.

So when I look at these estimates, I ask a few questions. First, what's the unit of output being measured? Is it a completed task in isolation, or progress on a project that unfolds over weeks? Second, does the measurement capture the downstream human steps, like checking, understanding and integrating what the AI produced? Often the human still needs to sleep on it before they really grasp it. Third, is the speedup measured on easy, well-specified tasks, where incubation matters little, and then extrapolated to research-level work, where it might matter a lot?

There's an important caveat in the other direction, though. This bottleneck applies to humans in the loop. If AI systems themselves are doing more of the end-to-end work, they don't need to sleep, and whatever function dreaming serves for us might be done differently, or not be needed at all. So the human-biology bottleneck is a strong reason to discount speedup claims for AI as a tool used by people. It's a much weaker reason to discount the possibility of rapid progress once humans are largely out of the loop. And I think that transition is exactly where a lot of the important uncertainty lies.

r001.rationale: The response explains that sleep and other human processes remain at biological speed, so accelerating the active work can yield far less overall progress than headline figures suggest. It explicitly says this is a reason to discount speedup claims when AI is used as a tool by people.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think this is actually a really important point, and it's one that often gets lost when people make these claims about AI speeding up human work by some factor. The question you have to ask is: what exactly is being sped up?

When someone says a tool makes a programmer twice as productive, the natural reading is that the programmer now gets twice as much done per day. But a day isn't entirely made up of the task that's being accelerated. There's sleep, there's eating, there's commuting, there's the meeting that was going to happen anyway, there's thinking about what the task even should be. If the AI only speeds up the typing-out-the-code part, and that was, say, a third of the actual working week, then even an infinite speed-up of that part gives you at most a fifty percent improvement overall. That's just Amdahl's law, really, from computer architecture: the gains are bounded by the fraction of the process you've actually touched.

So I think the first thing I'd do with any estimate is ask what fraction of the relevant process is being automated or accelerated, and then be quite suspicious of claims that treat a local speed-up as if it were a global one. And the second thing is that human work has these serial bottlenecks that don't compress. You mentioned sleep and dreaming, and I think that's a nice example because there's reasonable evidence that consolidation of ideas, the sort of incubation effect, actually depends on time passing and on sleep. You can't necessarily do a month's worth of reflective thinking in a day, even if your tools are fast, because the thinking has its own tempo. Similarly, if your work involves other people, it's bounded by their calendars and their attention. If it involves experiments in the real world, it's bounded by how long the cells take to grow or how long the regulator takes to reply.

Now, the interesting flip side is that this is exactly the reason people get excited about AI doing the work rather than merely assisting with it. If the AI is the one doing the research and it doesn't sleep, and you can run many copies of it in parallel, then a lot of those human-serial bottlenecks genuinely disappear. The speed-up there isn't two-x, it could in principle be enormous. But then the bottlenecks move. They move to the physical world, to compute, to data, to the parts of the process that still require a human to sign off or a lab to run something. And I think a lot of the disagreement about how fast things could go is really a disagreement about where those remaining bottlenecks are and how binding they are.

So my honest assessment is that the current per-worker speed-up numbers are probably modest and quite a bit smaller than the headline figures, precisely because of the things you mention. But I wouldn't take that as much comfort about the longer run, because the thing that could change the picture isn't making humans faster, it's removing the human from the loop in the places where the human was the slow part.

r001.rationale: The response explains that unaccelerated processes such as sleep and reflection limit overall gains, and warns against treating local AI speedups as global improvements in human work.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to be quite careful about what’s being sped up. If an AI lets you do a particular task ten times faster, that doesn’t mean you can achieve ten times as much over a year. The task may only occupy a small part of your time, and there may be other things you need to wait for.

Sleep is an interesting example because it’s not just downtime. Some of the work of learning and forming ideas seems to happen while we’re asleep, or when we’re thinking about something else. So if you compress all the explicit work into a much shorter period, it’s not obvious that you get the same result. You might have removed some of the time in which the understanding would have developed.

On the other hand, if the AI can perform that whole process itself, rather than merely assist a human with one part of it, then the human need for sleep may cease to be the relevant constraint. So I’d distinguish between speeding up tasks within a human workflow and replacing the workflow. For the former, I’d want to see measurements of completed projects, including the waiting and checking, rather than extrapolations from how quickly individual tasks can be done.

r001.rationale: The response says sleep and other waits can limit how much faster a human workflow becomes, but it does not suggest that AI speedup figures become irrelevant to assessing overall work acceleration.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to be quite careful about what’s being sped up. If AI makes a particular intellectual task ten times faster, that doesn’t mean that the whole process it’s part of becomes ten times faster. There may be other steps — sleeping on an idea, running an experiment, or waiting for someone else to make a decision — that haven’t changed at all.

Sleep is an interesting example because we don’t necessarily know which parts of it are essential to the intellectual work. Sometimes you go to bed with a problem and wake up with a solution. You can’t simply assume that making your conscious thinking faster would make that process faster too. But you also shouldn’t assume that an AI would need to reproduce the same biological process to get the same benefit.

So I’d want to distinguish speeding up individual tasks from speeding up an entire research project. The latter depends on where the bottlenecks are, and whether AI can remove them or find ways around them. A large improvement in one component can produce a surprisingly small improvement overall.

r001.rationale: The response says unchanged steps such as sleeping can prevent a faster intellectual task from speeding up the whole process, so task-level AI speedup figures may not reflect overall acceleration.
